recommendations.text: We suggest using motivational interviewing to increase engagement in treatment for tobacco and nicotine use.
We recommend the use of FDA-approved pharmacotherapies (e.g., bupropion sustained release, nicotine replacement therapy [NRT], and varenicline) for increasing abstinence from combustible tobacco.
For patients using nicotine replacement therapy (NRT), we recommend combination therapy (e.g., patch and short-acting NRT) over single NRT products for increasing abstinence from combustible tobacco.

For patients receiving a single medication, we recommend varenicline over other monotherapies (e.g., bupropion sustained release; single-agent nicotine replacement therapy [NRT]) for increasing abstinence from combustible tobacco.
In patients using bupropion sustained release, we suggest extending use beyond 12 weeks to maintain abstinence from combustible tobacco.

There is insufficient evidence to recommend for or against the extended use of varenicline or nicotine replacement therapy beyond standard duration of therapy (12 weeks) to achieve abstinence from combustible tobacco.
We suggest using varenicline or nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) for increasing abstinence from electronic nicotine delivery systems (ENDS).
We suggest using nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) for increasing abstinence from smokeless tobacco.
We recommend using varenicline for increasing abstinence from smokeless tobacco.
We suggest varenicline be started prior to surgery to assist patients in quitting tobacco use.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend for or against the use of nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) or bupropion for tobacco cessation in the perioperative period.

We suggest against electronic nicotine delivery systems (ENDS) products for improving abstinence from tobacco and nicotine products. (ENDS is classified as a tobacco product and is not FDA approved for any use)
We recommend more intensive behavioral counseling (at least four encounters) as compared to less intensive counseling to increase abstinence from tobacco and nicotine products.
We suggest using text messaging (SMS) programs to increase abstinence from tobacco and nicotine products.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend any specific behavioral counseling intervention over standard cognitive behavior therapy for tobacco cessation.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend for or against adding lifestyle interventions (e.g., diet, exercise) to behavioral counseling for tobacco cessation.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend either for or against smartphone apps for increasing abstinence from tobacco and nicotine products.
If patients return to tobacco use, we suggest immediate repeat treatment with pharmacotherapy and counseling.
In patients not ready to quit (e.g., in the next 30 days), we suggest nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) to increase quit attempts.
In patients not ready to quit (e.g., in the next 30 days), we suggest varenicline to increase quit attempts and abstinence from tobacco and nicotine products.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend either for or against medication sampling for increasing treatment engagement.
In patients with stable mental health conditions, we suggest treating tobacco use with pharmacotherapy.
In patients with stable mental health conditions, we recommend varenicline over single agent nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) or bupropion sustained release to improve continuous abstinence.
We suggest counseling be adapted to address both tobacco use and co-occurring serious mental illness (e.g., bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, other psychotic disorders).
In patients being treated for alcohol use disorder/substance use disorder, we suggest concurrently treating tobacco use with behavioral counseling and pharmacotherapy.

There is insufficient evidence to recommend for or against counseling that combines treatment for tobacco use and depression or post-traumatic stress disorder compared to standard tobacco cessation counseling.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend for or against the effectiveness of bupropion or nicotine replacement therapy for tobacco cessation during pregnancy.
As a standalone therapy, we suggest against acupuncture, mindfulness, or hypnotherapy for abstinence from tobacco and nicotine products.

There is insufficient evidence to recommend either for or against repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, transcranial direct current stimulation, and intermittent theta burst stimulation for abstinence from tobacco and nicotine products, reduced use, or cravings.
We recommend using proactive outreach to increase engagement in treatment for tobacco and nicotine use.
We suggest the use of contingency management or incentives in combination with behavioral counseling and pharmacotherapy for treating tobacco and nicotine use.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend either for or against the use of an opt-out approach to increase engagement in treatment for tobacco and nicotine use.
